passages.t: ‘Do not fret’, and ‘the meek will inherit the land’
passages.happening:
The heading reads, “Of David” (verse 1). The psalm opens with advice: “Do not fret over those who do evil; do not envy those who do wrong” (verse 1). The reason is that their success will not last. “For they wither quickly like grass and wilt like tender plants” (verse 2).

Then a string of instructions for the person who trusts God. “Trust in the LORD and do good; dwell in the land and cultivate faithfulness” (verse 3). “Delight yourself in the LORD, and He will give you the desires of your heart” (verse 4). “Commit your way to the LORD; trust in Him, and He will do it” (verse 5). “Be still before the LORD and wait patiently for Him” (verse 7).

“Refrain from anger and abandon wrath” (verse 8). “Yet a little while, and the wicked will be no more” (verse 10). “But the meek will inherit the land and delight in abundant prosperity” (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
Psalm 37 is a wisdom psalm, like the book of Proverbs. It speaks to people rather than to God. It is also an alphabet poem, roughly every second verse beginning with the next Hebrew letter, so it reads like a teacher's list of sayings.

‘Fret’ means to get heated, to burn up inside. Three times in eight verses the psalm says ‘do not fret’ (verses 1, 7 and 8). The problem it faces is old and ordinary: good people stay poor while cheats get rich.

‘The land’ meant a family's share of farmland. In Israel the land was God's gift, divided among the families, and meant to stay in the family. But powerful people often took the land of the weak, as the prophets complained. To a poor family, ‘inherit the land’ meant: you will not lose your home and fields.

‘The meek’ are the lowly and humble, people without power, who do not grab.

Grass in that land springs up green after the winter rains and dries up in a few weeks of heat. The wicked look strong. They are as lasting as grass.
passages.later:
Jesus took up verse 11 in the Sermon on the Mount: “Blessed are the meek, for they will inherit the earth” (Matthew 5:5). His words are almost the same as the Greek translation of the psalm. The Hebrew word for ‘land’ can also mean ‘earth’, and in Jesus' mouth the promise grows to the whole earth made new.

Paul says Abraham's children are heirs “of the world” (Romans 4:13), and Peter looks for “a new heaven and a new earth, where righteousness dwells” (2 Peter 3:13).

Verse 5's ‘commit your way’ is echoed by Peter: “Cast all your anxiety on Him, because He cares for you” (1 Peter 5:7).
passages.hard:
‘He will give you the desires of your heart’ (verse 4). Does that mean God will give you whatever you want if you are religious enough?

No. The first half of the verse comes first: ‘Delight yourself in the LORD.’ When God himself is your delight, your desires change. The promise is not a trick for getting things. It is a picture of a heart that wants God most, and finds that he does not disappoint.
passages.asks:
What makes you fret? Name the person or the unfairness that keeps you burning inside. The psalm does not say it does not matter. It says your anger will not fix it, and God will.

Try verse 7 for a week: ‘Be still before the LORD and wait patiently for Him.’ Stillness is not doing nothing. It is refusing to be pushed by envy.

passages.t: ‘Better is the little of the righteous’, and ‘I once was young’
passages.happening:
The wicked plot against the righteous, “but the Lord laughs, seeing that their day is coming” (verse 13). Their weapons turn on them: “their swords will pierce their own hearts” (verse 15).

“Better is the little of the righteous than the abundance of many who are wicked” (verse 16). The righteous are kept even in hard times: “in the days of famine they will be satisfied” (verse 19). “The wicked borrow and do not repay, but the righteous are gracious and giving” (verse 21).

Even a fall is not the end. “Though he falls, he will not be overwhelmed, for the LORD is holding his hand” (verse 24).

Then an old man speaks from long life: “I once was young and now am old, yet never have I seen the righteous abandoned or their children begging for bread” (verse 25).
passages.hearers:
Borrowing and lending were part of village life. In a bad year a family might need a loan of grain to survive. The law forbade charging interest to a neighbour in need (Exodus 22:25). So the generous lender of verses 21 and 26 is a person who helps neighbours through hard seasons.

‘The Lord laughs’ (verse 13) is not cruelty. It is the calm of someone who knows how the story ends. Psalm 2 uses the same picture.

‘Holding his hand’ (verse 24) is a picture from walking: a parent with a child on rough ground. The child may trip. The hand does not let go.
passages.later:
Jesus told of a poor man, Lazarus, who lay at a rich man's gate “longing to be fed with the crumbs that fell from the rich man's table” (Luke 16:21). It was Lazarus, not the rich man, who was carried to Abraham's side.

The early church knew famine. When one struck in the time of the emperor Claudius, the disciples “decided to send relief to the brothers living in Judea” (Acts 11:29). Believers went hungry, and other believers fed them.

James writes, “Has not God chosen the poor of this world to be rich in faith” (James 2:5).
passages.hard:
‘Never have I seen the righteous abandoned or their children begging for bread’ (verse 25). But faithful people do sometimes go hungry. Their children do sometimes beg. Is the psalm simply wrong?

It is honest to say plainly: the righteous do sometimes go hungry. The Bible itself says so. A famine drove Naomi's family, faithful Israelites, out of Bethlehem (Ruth 1:1). Lazarus was a beggar. The believers in Judea needed relief.

Readers have understood verse 25 in several ways. It is one old man's witness to what he saw in his own life, not a promise for every life. It describes how God's world usually works when a community keeps his law: the generous are helped by others when trouble comes. And it looks ahead to the end of the story, when God will put right what is wrong.

One use of the verse is ruled out. It must never be used to say that poor people are poor because they are not righteous. The rest of Scripture rejects that.

The psalm's question gets a deeper answer in Psalm 73. There a man almost lost his faith watching the wicked prosper, “until I entered God's sanctuary; then I discerned their end” (Psalm 73:17). And he found that God himself was his portion when everything else failed (Psalm 73:26).
passages.asks:
Verse 16 asks what you count as rich. ‘The little of the righteous’ is better than a fortune gained by wrong.

And if you are one of the righteous who has gone hungry, the psalm does not ask you to pretend. It asks you to keep hold of the hand that holds yours (verse 24), and it asks the rest of God's people to be the open hand that feeds you (verse 26).

passages.t: ‘Wait for the LORD and keep His way’, and the tree that vanished
passages.happening:
The teacher repeats his call. “Turn away from evil and do good, so that you will abide forever” (verse 27). “For the LORD loves justice and will not forsake His saints” (verse 28). “The righteous will inherit the land and dwell in it forever” (verse 29).

The good person's words and steps come from God's teaching. “The law of his God is in his heart; his steps do not falter” (verse 31).

“Wait for the LORD and keep His way, and He will raise you up to inherit the land” (verse 34).

Then a story from his own eyes. “I have seen a wicked, ruthless man flourishing like a well-rooted native tree, yet he passed away and was no more; though I searched, he could not be found” (verses 35-36).

It ends, “The salvation of the righteous is from the LORD; He is their stronghold in time of trouble” (verse 39).
passages.hearers:
‘Inherit the land’ comes five times in the psalm (verses 9, 11, 22, 29 and 34). It is the psalm's drumbeat. To poor farmers afraid of losing everything, it was the promise they needed most.

The tree of verse 35 is a native tree, deep-rooted, the kind that looks as if it will stand for ever. Then one day it is gone. The wicked man's success looked just as permanent.

‘The law of his God is in his heart’ (verse 31) links back to Psalm 1, where the happy person delights in God's teaching. Wisdom here is not cleverness. It is a heart shaped by God's word.
passages.later:
God promised through Jeremiah a day when he would write his law on hearts (Jeremiah 31:33), what verse 31 describes.

Hebrews says the faithful of old “died in faith, without having received the things they were promised” and saw them “from afar” (Hebrews 11:13). The promise of the land was larger than any field. Revelation sees its end: “a new heaven and a new earth” (Revelation 21:1).

Jesus said, “Do not store up for yourselves treasures on earth” (Matthew 6:19). The wicked man's tree is a picture of why.
passages.asks:
The psalm asks for patience over a long time. It does not promise that the wrong will be put right by Friday. It asks you to keep God's way while you wait.

Notice also verse 31. The person who waits well is the person whose heart is full of God's word. Patience grows from what you feed on.
